Yes, I put that link down because I suspect except DataBricks guys and those follow the news announcements, quite some may be unaware of that project exists (They just open source it months after their initial presentation). There may be something to 'share' in terms of higher level interface.

Went to quite a number of Berkeley R and SF R meetups and notice there is a quite some "information /cultural gap" between software engineers and R Statisticians (not Machine Learning):

  • most of the experienced R guys (refer to "they" hereafter) are unaware of R on Spark
  • those who are aware deeply believe they have to use Java/Python to use Spark.
  • they find ML libraries from Python and Java only contain the basic algorithms; and is insufficient for their daily work
  • those who do use, some are concern that Libraries from other ecosystem is not rigorously 'Peer-reviewed'
  • lots of latest methods are published in R and with the paper;
  • R, to them, goes from data munging to publishing (for internal meetings quickly - cycle ranging from days/1-2 week time frame), Public facing data viz, leave that to software developers. So another disincentive to learn other language.
  • want to keep their R way of doing thing, and very importantly able to use the other R packages.
  • unlike other ecosystems, there are SO MANY STYLES depending on what R packages to use (for examples data.frame, plyr, dplyr, sqldf, data.table etc), Learn another language not top of their list.
  • most of their time is spent on exploring new and tweaking existing model, they rely on sampling to do their work to proceed and literately quickly. Processing all data is not top of their list.
  • they are behind programmers ways of working (like git or even source control etc). Only recently aware of considering making R packages etc

Re: Data Frame abstraction layer for RDD

DDF project uses SQL mapping or extract RDD and work on RDD so they have flexibility. The idea is that when you are doing simple SQL like manipulations, by mapping them to SQL one can unleash the query optimizer, for instance changing the order of a where vs a select. If select and where are implemented as R functions, those would be black box to any optimizer I can think of. On the other hand one in R may do thing like group data by user-id and then fit a linear model to each group and I don't think you can do that by SQL mapping, unless UDF have become more powerful since I last checked. I wrote a package to support data frames on top of sparkR where the goal was to show the API possibilities more than utter efficiency – will not work well for small reduce groups. See RevolutionAnalytics/plyrmr on github. Originally developed for Hadoop MR now has a partial spark backend. You all know what has been said about premature optimization. I think mapping to SQL is premature optimization. First implement, say, filter, like plyrmr does, executing R functions on chunks of data. Then map the simple case to SQL for max speed, transparently for user. Doing only SQL operations in R is not in keeping with the statistical focus of the language IMHO.

messages.author: c7ffcfaebad9edef
messages.subject: [JIRA] (SPARKR-1) Data Frame abstraction layer for RDD
parts: Shivaram Venkataraman commented on SPARKR-1
Re: Data Frame abstraction layer for RDD

Thanks everybody for your comments on this issue. One of the goals of the SparkR project has been to closely mirror the main Spark project so as to avoid reimplementing things. Most recently there has been a new feature merged into Apache Spark that adds support for DataFrames in Scala and Python SPARK-5097.

Thus I think the most natural way forward for SparkR is to integrate with the DataFrame backend in Scala. This will gives us a bunch of advantages where the SparkSQL query optimizer can appropriately optimize the column selections / operations and from an R side we only need to think about translating the operators to match the backing DataFrame.

I'm going to break down some sub-tasks for this effort and link it to this issue. The one catch with this is that the Scala DataFrame is only available in Spark 1.3, so we will probably do development on this in a separate branch and merge the branch in after 1.3 is released.
